extracted.intended_audience: K-12 mathematics teachers, pre-service teachers, and teacher educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for integrating history of mathematics into classroom teaching to increase relevance, motivation, and understanding; includes suggested strategies, examples, and recommended teacher outcomes. Targets teachers and teacher-preparation programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance in mathematics teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance implies understanding, importance, and appreciation—features that should always permeate mathematics teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical material to answer students' question 'What is this stuff good for?' by making mathematics feel relevant; design lessons so relevance (understanding, importance, appreciation) is explicit rather than assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray mathematics as a human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: History reveals to students that mathematics is a human activity; such a recognition could allay mathematical anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce biographical, cultural, or situational historical contexts that show mathematicians as people working in response to problems, thereby reducing intimidation and helping students relate to mathematics emotionally and socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate historical content naturally to show evolution of concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural integration of historical content into mathematics courses demonstrates to students that the discipline is both constantly evolving and contains concepts that echo across time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed historical threads into regular topics (e.g., how a concept developed, multiple historical solutions) rather than treating history as an add-on; emphasize continuity and change to deepen conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of teaching strategies grounded in history
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply a variety of teaching strategies to accomplish incorporation of historical background in classroom mathematics (e.g., problems, exercises, activities, workbooks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ multiple formats—short reading, primary-source problems, workbook activities, class discussion, project work—to suit different levels and learning goals. The article cites publications (e.g., Learning Activities from the History of Mathematics, Mathematical Expeditions) as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select historical problems accessible to students
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose historical problems and exercises that are within the capacity of modern high school (or target grade) students and that add intrigue and motivation (e.g., Old Babylonian scribal problems, Luoshu magic square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tasks that are mathematically meaningful but not beyond students' skills; use the historical context to increase engagement. Example: a Babylonian tablet problem about areas that can be tackled with contemporary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect historical examples to societal needs and cause-effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use historical problems as 'instances of cause and effect, the needs of society, and the attempts to apply mathematics to satisfy those needs' so students see why mathematics developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a historical topic, explicitly discuss the practical problem that motivated the mathematics (e.g., commerce, engineering, astronomy) to highlight application and origin of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diverse cultural and gender perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop an appreciation of the contributions made by various cultures to the growth and development of mathematical ideas; investigate contributions made by individuals, both female and male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select examples from multiple cultures and highlight women mathematicians and lesser-known contributors to counteract prejudicial ignorance and broaden students' perspectives; the article notes expanded recognition of non-Western contributions and women's achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach historical development of core concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain an understanding of the historical development of major school mathematics concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure lessons so students learn not only the concept and procedure but also its historical genesis and evolution; this is an explicit recommendation from teacher-preparation standards cited in the article (MAA Committee report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use primary historical sources in instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate primary historical sources (e.g., tablets, original texts) as part of classroom instruction and teacher enrichment projects (e.g., TRIUMPHS) to transform instruction via primary historical sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, employ facsimiles, translations, or curated excerpts of primary documents to allow students to interact with authentic material; projects and journals (Convergence, TRIUMPHS) provide models and curated sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage curated resources and teacher-focused publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and adapt resources from journals, books, and manuals that present historical mathematics material and classroom activities (e.g., Convergence, Mathematical Expeditions, Learning Activities from the History of Mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult established compilations and repositories to find vetted problems, lesson plans, and background; republished articles and teacher manuals can provide ready-to-use activities and further references.
